# Statistical Inference


**Week 5** - A refresher of regression, two independent samples t-test and 
one-way ANOVA

In this workshop, you will review three statistical inference techniques used in 
analysing simple data sets. These methods are simple regression with a single 
numeric (and preferably) continuous explanatory variable, the two independent 
samples t-test and one-way ANOVA.

Workshop materials are available in the github repository [ECS200](https://github.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop).

![](images/base_model.png)

Today's task will be a refresher on the following:

- Regression
- Two independent samples t-test
- One-way ANOVA

For each, you will need to understand about intercepts, slopes, p-values, 
assumptions of **equal variances**, assumptions of **independence**, and 
assumptions that the **residuals** have a normal distribution.

# Background {.unnumbered}

## Is your data linear? {.unnumbered}

This app below fits a straight-line (ordinary least squares) regression to 
simulated data using the `lm()` function (`lm(y ~ x, data = mydata)`), and displays 
three diagnostic plots to help you judge whether that line is an appropriate summary 
of the relationship.

You can choose from five data patterns - linear up, linear down, curved up, 
curved down, and fan-shaped

You can toggle residual lines on or off. Pressing `Resample` generates a fresh 
dataset from the same pattern so you can see how much the plots vary by chance.

The diagnostic plots:

- **Scatter plot** with the fitted regression line (and optional residuals)
- **Residuals vs. Fitted** — should show no pattern if the linear model fits. 
Patterns (e.g., curves) suggest model misspecification, such as non-linearity 
(e.g. try curve up or curve down). Points far from zero indicate large residuals 
(potential outliers). 
Clusters or structure imply the model is not capturing systematic variation.
- **Normal Q-Q** — checks whether residuals follow a normal distribution. Systematic deviations 
(S-shape or heavy tails) indicate non-normal residuals. Extreme points far from 
the line suggest outliers or influential observations. Departures mainly at the 
ends indicate issues in the tails rather than the center.

### How to use {.unnumbered}

1. Select a trend from the radio buttons on the left.
2. Toggle Show residuals to see how far each point sits from the line.
3. Press `Resample` to draw a new dataset and observe natural sampling variation.
4. Compare the two diagnostic plots to the ideal (random scatter, straight Q-Q line).


```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 700
library(shiny)
library(bslib)

# ---------------------------
# Data generator
# ---------------------------
draw.data <- function(type) {
  
  n <- 250
  
  if (type == "linear.up") {
    x <- c(runif(n-2, 0, 4), 2, 2.1)
    y <- 2*x + rnorm(n, sd=2)
  }
  if (type == "linear.down") {
    x <- c(runif(n-2, 0, 4), 2, 2.1)
    y <- -2*x + rnorm(n, sd=2)
  }
  if (type == "curved.up") {
    x <- c(runif(n-2, 0, 4), 2, 2.1)
    y <- 2*x^4 + rnorm(n, sd=16)
  }
  if (type == "curved.down") {
    x <- c(runif(n-2, 0, 4), 2, 2.1)
    y <- -2*x^3 + rnorm(n, sd=9)
  }
  if (type == "fan.shaped") {
    x <- seq(0, 3.99, 4/n)
    y <- c(rnorm(n/8,3,1), rnorm(n/8,3.5,2), rnorm(n/8,4,2.5),
           rnorm(n/8,4.5,3), rnorm(n/4,5,4), rnorm((n/4)+2,6,5))
  }
  
  data.frame(x=x, y=y)
}

# ---------------------------
# UI
# ---------------------------
ui <- pageWithSidebar(
  
  headerPanel(""),
  
  sidebarPanel(
    
    radioButtons("type", "Select a trend:",
                 list("Linear up"    = "linear.up",
                      "Linear down"  = "linear.down",
                      "Curved up"    = "curved.up",
                      "Curved down"  = "curved.down",
                      "Fan-shaped"   = "fan.shaped")),
    br(),
    
    checkboxInput("show.resid", "Show residuals", FALSE),
    
    br(),
    
    actionButton("resample", "Resample", class = "btn-primary", style = "background-color: #e82c4a"),
    
    br()
    
  ),

  
  mainPanel(
    plotOutput("scatter"),
    br(),
    br(),
    plotOutput("residuals")
  )
)

# ---------------------------
# SERVER
# ---------------------------
server <- function(input, output) {
  
  mydata <- reactive({
    input$resample        # dependency trigger
    draw.data(input$type)
  })
  
  lmResults <- reactive({
    lm(y ~ x, data = mydata())
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Scatter plot with regression line, CI, PI, optional residuals
  # ---------------------------
  output$scatter <- renderPlot({
    
    data1 <- mydata()
    x     <- data1$x
    y     <- data1$y
    
    xcon      <- seq(min(x) - 0.1, max(x) + 0.1, 0.025)
    predictor <- data.frame(x = xcon)
    
    yhat  <- predict(lmResults())
    yline <- predict(lmResults(), predictor)
    
    newx  <- seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 200)
    confs <- predict(lmResults(), newdata = data.frame(x = newx),
                     interval = "confidence")
    preds <- predict(lmResults(), newdata = data.frame(x = newx),
                     interval = "predict")
    
    r.squared <- round(summary(lmResults())$r.squared, 4)
    corr.coef <- round(sqrt(r.squared), 4)
    
    par(cex.main = 1.2, cex.lab = 1.2, cex.axis = 1.2, mar = c(4,4,4,1))
    
    plot(c(min(x), max(x)),
         c(min(y, yline), max(y, yline)),
         type = "n",
         xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
         main = paste0("Regression Model\n",
                       "(R = ", corr.coef, ", R-squared = ", r.squared, ")"))
    
    # Prediction interval band (lighter)
    polygon(c(rev(newx), newx),
            c(rev(preds[, 3]), preds[, 2]),
            col = grey(0.95), border = NA)
    
    # Confidence interval band (darker)
    polygon(c(rev(newx), newx),
            c(rev(confs[, 3]), confs[, 2]),
            col = grey(0.75), border = NA)
    
    points(x, y, pch = 19, col = "#e82c4a")
    lines(xcon, yline, lwd = 2, col = "black")
    
    # Optional residual lines
    if (input$show.resid)
      for (j in seq_along(x))
        lines(rep(x[j], 2), c(yhat[j], y[j]), col = "#e82c4a")
    
    legend_pos <- ifelse(lmResults()$coefficients[1] < 1, "topleft", "topright")
    if (input$type == "linear.down") legend_pos <- "topright"
    if (input$type == "fan.shaped")  legend_pos <- "topleft"
    
    legend(legend_pos, inset = 0.05,
           legend = c("Regression Line", "Confidence Interval", "Prediction Interval"),
           fill   = c("black", grey(0.75), grey(0.95)))
    box()
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Diagnostic plots: residuals vs fitted, histogram, Q-Q
  # ---------------------------
  output$residuals <- renderPlot({
    
    residuals <- summary(lmResults())$residuals
    predicted <- predict(lmResults(), newdata = data.frame(x = mydata()$x))
    
    par(mfrow = c(1,2), # two plots appear side by side
        cex.main = 1.2, # plot title 1.5 times larger
        cex.lab = 1.2, # x and y labels 1.5 times larger
        cex.axis = 1.2, # axis numbers 1.5 times larger
        mar = c(4,5,2,2)) # Sets plot margins (in lines of text) in the order: bottom, left, top, right.
    
    # Residuals vs Fitted
    plot(residuals ~ predicted,
         main = "Residuals vs. Fitted Values",
         xlab = "Fitted Values", ylab = "Residuals",
         pch = 19, col = "#e82c4a")
    abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "black")
    
    # Histogram of residuals with density overlay
    
    #d <- density(residuals)
    #h <- hist(residuals, plot = FALSE)
    #hist(residuals,
    #     main = "Histogram of Residuals", xlab = "Residuals",
    #     col  = "#569BBDC0", prob = TRUE,
    #     ylim = c(0, max(max(d$y), max(h$density))))
    #lines(d, col = "#569BBD", lwd = 2)
    
    # Normal Q-Q plot
    qqnorm(residuals, pch = 19, col = "#e82c4a",
           main = "Normal Q-Q Plot of Residuals")
    qqline(residuals, col = "black", lwd = 2)
    
  }, height = 250)
}

shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

```
  
  
## Model Assumptions {.unnumbered}

We will include two more diagnostic plot on top of the Residuals vs. Fitted, and 
Normal Q-Q, which is called the **Scale-Location** plot which checks for unequal 
spread (heteroscedasticity), and **Leverage** plot which visualises how unusual a 
point's x-value is relative to the rest of the data.

In this app below, a single <span style="color:#e82c4a;">red</span> point sits among 
a cloud of black data points. You can click anywhere on the scatter plot to move 
the <span style="color:#e82c4a;">red</span> point and instantly see how the 
fitted regression line responds. Three standard diagnostic plots update in real 
time so you can watch leverage and influence change as you drag the point to different 
positions.

The additional diagnostic plots:

- **Scale-Location**: Look for constant spread. A funnel (increasing spread) 
indicates heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance). Horizontal banding is ideal. 
If variance increases with fitted values, model assumptions are violated.
- High leverage + large residual = **influential**. Leverage threshold = 2 × mean 
leverage ≈ 0.068. Leverage reflects how extreme a point is in x-space.
High leverage alone is not problematic unless paired with a large residual.
Points with high leverage and large residuals are most concerning.

### How to use {.unnumbered}

1. Set the sample size with the slider and press `Resample` for a new dataset.
2. Click anywhere on the left-hand scatter plot to move the <span style="color:#e82c4a;">red</span> point.
3. Choose a diagnostic plot from the radio buttons to see how that measure changes.
4. Switch between fitting the model to all data (<span style="color:#e82c4a;">red</span> 
point included) or black points only to compare the two fitted lines.

```{shinylive-r}
#| standalone: true
#| viewerHeight: 600

# ---------------------------
# Data generator
# ---------------------------
generate_data <- function(n) {
  x      <- 1:n
  y      <- x + rnorm(n, sd = n / 4)
  colour <- rep("black", n)
  
  x      <- c(x, mean(x))
  y      <- c(y, mean(y))
  colour <- c(colour, "#e82c4a")
  
  data.frame(x = x, y = y, colour = colour,
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

# ---------------------------
# UI
# ---------------------------
ui <- fluidPage(
  
  tags$head(
    tags$style(HTML("
      .sidebar {
        background-color: #f7f7f7;
        padding: 15px;
        border-radius: 8px;
        border: 1px solid #ddd;
      }
      #resample {
        background-color: #e82c4a;
        color: white;
        border: none;
        padding: 6px 12px;
        margin-top: 4px;
        margin-bottom: 10px;
        font-size: 14px;
      }
      #resample:hover {
        background-color: #3E7C99;
        color: white;
      }
      #resample:active {
        transform: scale(0.97);
      }
    "))
  ),
  
  fluidRow(
    
    # ---------------------------
    # SIDEBAR
    # ---------------------------
    column(
      width = 3,
      div(class = "sidebar",
          
          sliderInput("sample_size", "Sample size:",
                      min = 5, max = 100, value = 10),
          
          actionButton("resample", "Resample", style = "background-color: #e82c4a"),
          
          tags$hr(),
          
          radioButtons("choice", "Diagnostic to plot",
                       choiceNames = c(
                         "Residual vs. Fitted",

                       ),

                       selected = 1),
          
          radioButtons("model_choice", "Model",
                       choices = c(
                         "All data (red point included)" = "all",

                       ),
                       selected = "all"),
          
      )
    ),
    
    # ---------------------------
    # MAIN PANEL

    column(
      width = 9,
      fluidRow(
        
        # Left: raw data plot + summary table
        column(
          width = 6,
          plotOutput("rawPlot", height = "400px", click = "plot_click"),
          tags$div(
            style = "background-color:#f9f9f9;
                     padding:12px;

          )
        ),

          tags$div(
            style = "background-color:#f9f9f9;

# ---------------------------
# SERVER
# ---------------------------
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  
  diag_titles <- c(
    "Residual vs. Fitted",
    "Normal Q-Q",
    "Scale-Location",
    "Residual vs Leverage"
  )
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Reactive data store
  # ---------------------------
  plot_data <- reactiveVal(generate_data(10))
  
  observeEvent(input$sample_size, {
    plot_data(generate_data(input$sample_size))
  })
  
  observeEvent(input$resample, {
    plot_data(generate_data(input$sample_size))
  })
  
  # Clicking the raw plot moves the red point
  observeEvent(input$plot_click, {
    dat <- plot_data()
    dat[nrow(dat), "x"] <- input$plot_click$x
    dat[nrow(dat), "y"] <- input$plot_click$y
    plot_data(dat)
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Fitted models
  # ---------------------------
  mods <- reactive({
    dat <- plot_data()
    req(nrow(dat) > 2)
    list(
      mod_all   = lm(y ~ x, data = dat),
      mod_black = lm(y ~ x, data = dat[dat$colour == "black", ])
    )
  })
  
  # Active model (based on radio button)
  active_mod <- reactive({
    if (input$model_choice == "all") mods()$mod_all else mods()$mod_black
  })
  
  model_label <- reactive({
    if (input$model_choice == "all") " — All" else " — Black"
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Raw data plot (base R)
  # ---------------------------
  output$rawPlot <- renderPlot({
    
    dat    <- plot_data()
    black  <- dat[dat$colour == "black", ]
    red    <- dat[dat$colour == "#e82c4a",   ]
    
    n      <- input$sample_size
    xlim   <- c(min(dat$x) - n,     max(dat$x) + n)
    ylim   <- c(min(dat$y) - 2 * n, max(dat$y) + 2 * n)
    
    # Helper: compute 95% CI band over a fine x grid for a given model
    ci_band <- function(mod, x_seq) {
      as.data.frame(predict(mod,
                            newdata = data.frame(x = x_seq),
                            interval = "confidence",
                            level    = 0.95))
    }
    
    x_seq     <- seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 200)
    ci_all    <- ci_band(mods()$mod_all,   x_seq)
    ci_black  <- ci_band(mods()$mod_black, x_seq)
    
    plot(dat$x, dat$y,
         col  = dat$colour,
         pch  = ifelse(dat$colour == "#e82c4a", 17, 16),
         cex  = ifelse(dat$colour == "#e82c4a", 2,  1.2),
         xlim = xlim, ylim = ylim,
         xlab = "x", ylab = "y",
         main = paste0("Data and fitted regression lines", model_label()),
         las  = 1)
    
    # Shaded 95% CI — all data (red, semi-transparent)
    polygon(c(x_seq, rev(x_seq)),
            c(ci_all$lwr, rev(ci_all$upr)),
            col    = adjustcolor("#e82c4a",   alpha.f = 0.15),
            border = NA)
    
    # Shaded 95% CI — black only (grey, semi-transparent)
    polygon(c(x_seq, rev(x_seq)),
            c(ci_black$lwr, rev(ci_black$upr)),
            col    = adjustcolor("black", alpha.f = 0.10),
            border = NA)
    
    # Regression lines
    lines(x_seq, ci_all$fit,   col = "#e82c4a",   lwd = 2)
    lines(x_seq, ci_black$fit, col = "black", lwd = 2)
    
    # Redraw points on top of shaded bands
    points(dat$x, dat$y,
           col = dat$colour,
           pch = ifelse(dat$colour == "#e82c4a", 17, 16),
           cex = ifelse(dat$colour == "#e82c4a", 2,  1.2))
    
    legend("topleft",
           legend = c("All data fit", "Black only fit", "Influential point"),
           col    = c("#e82c4a", "black", "#e82c4a"),
           lty    = c(1, 1, NA),
           pch    = c(NA, NA, 17),
           lwd    = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Summary table
  # ---------------------------
  output$effect_table <- renderTable({
    
    req(mods())
    dat     <- plot_data()
    n_black <- sum(dat$colour == "black")
    n_all   <- nrow(dat)
    
    cf_all   <- coef(mods()$mod_all)
    cf_black <- coef(mods()$mod_black)
    r2_all   <- summary(mods()$mod_all)$r.squared
    r2_black <- summary(mods()$mod_black)$r.squared
    
    df <- data.frame(
      Model     = c("All data", "Black only", "\u0394 (All \u2212 Black)"),
      n         = c(n_all, n_black, n_all - n_black),
      Intercept = c(cf_all["(Intercept)"],
                    cf_black["(Intercept)"],
                    cf_all["(Intercept)"] - cf_black["(Intercept)"]),
      Slope     = c(cf_all["x"],
                    cf_black["x"],
                    cf_all["x"] - cf_black["x"]),
      R2        = c(r2_all, r2_black, r2_all - r2_black),
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
    df
    
  }, digits = 3)
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Diagnostic data
  # ---------------------------
  diag_data <- reactive({
    
    mod <- active_mod()
    dat <- plot_data()
    n   <- length(resid(mod))
    
    fitted_vals <- fitted(mod)
    resids      <- resid(mod)
    std_resids  <- rstandard(mod)
    cooksd      <- cooks.distance(mod)
    hat         <- hatvalues(mod)
    
    lev_thresh  <- 2 * mean(hat)
    cook_thresh <- 4 / n
    
    # Index of the red point within this model's data.
    # integer(0) when black-only model is active — no red point present.
    if (input$model_choice == "all") {
      red_idx <- which(dat$colour == "#e82c4a")
    } else {
      red_idx <- integer(0)
    }
    
    list(
      df = data.frame(
        obs           = seq_along(fitted_vals),
        fitted        = fitted_vals,
        resid         = resids,
        stdresid      = std_resids,
        cooksd        = cooksd,
        hat           = hat,
        high_leverage = hat    > lev_thresh,
        high_cook     = cooksd > cook_thresh,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ),
      red_idx = red_idx
    )
  })
  
  # ---------------------------
  # Diagnostic plots (base R)
  # ---------------------------
  output$diagnostic_plot <- renderPlot({
    
    req(mods())
    dd      <- diag_data()
    d       <- dd$df
    ri      <- dd$red_idx          # row index of red point; integer(0) if absent
    has_red <- length(ri) > 0
    
    choice <- as.numeric(input$choice)
    title  <- paste0(diag_titles[choice], model_label())
    
    # Overlay the red triangle — called after each plot is drawn
    mark_red <- function(x_val, y_val) {
      points(x_val, y_val, col = "#e82c4a", pch = 17, cex = 2)
    }
    
    # ── 1: Residual vs Fitted ──────────────────────────────────
    if (choice == 1) {
      plot(d$fitted, d$resid,
           xlab = "Fitted values", ylab = "Residuals",
           main = title, pch = 16, col = "black", las = 1)
      abline(h = 0, lty = 2, col = "grey50")
      lines(lowess(d$fitted, d$resid), col = "#e82c4a", lwd = 2)
      if (has_red) mark_red(d$fitted[ri], d$resid[ri])
    }
    
    # ── 2: Normal Q-Q ─────────────────────────────────────────
    if (choice == 2) {
      # qqnorm invisibly returns the plotted (x, y) coordinates
      # in the same row-order as the input, so [ri] is safe
      qq <- qqnorm(d$stdresid, main = title,
                   pch = 16, col = "black", las = 1)
      qqline(d$stdresid, col = "#e82c4a", lwd = 2)
      if (has_red) mark_red(qq$x[ri], qq$y[ri])
    }
    
    # ── 3: Scale-Location ─────────────────────────────────────
    if (choice == 3) {
      sqrt_abs_resid <- sqrt(abs(d$stdresid))
      plot(d$fitted, sqrt_abs_resid,
           xlab = "Fitted values",
           ylab = expression(sqrt("|Standardised residuals|")),
           main = title, pch = 16, col = "black", las = 1)
      lines(lowess(d$fitted, sqrt_abs_resid), col = "#e82c4a", lwd = 2)
      if (has_red) mark_red(d$fitted[ri], sqrt_abs_resid[ri])
    }
    
    # ── 4: Residual vs Leverage ───────────────────────────────
    if (choice == 4) {
      lev_thresh <- 2 * mean(d$hat)
      plot(d$hat, d$stdresid,
           xlab = "Leverage", ylab = "Standardised residuals",
           main = title, pch = 16, col = "black", las = 1)
      abline(h = 0,          lty = 2, col = "grey50")
      abline(v = lev_thresh, lty = 2, col = "#e82c4a", lwd = 1.5)
      if (has_red) mark_red(d$hat[ri], d$stdresid[ri])
      legend("topright",
             legend = paste0("Leverage threshold = ", round(lev_thresh, 3)),
             lty = 2, col = "#e82c4a", bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
    }
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)

```


# Topics {.unnumbered}

::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

## Regression

Simple linear regression is a statistical technique used to describe and quantify 
the relationship between **two numeric (and preferably continuous) variables**. 
In ecological research, it is commonly applied to examine how an environmental 
predictor influences a biological response. For example, an ecologist may wish to 
determine whether plant biomass increases with soil nitrogen availability or 
whether bird abundance declines as distance from a forest edge increases. We will 
explore more complex regression modelling, later in the unit. 

In this example with the cleaned version of the `plant_calcium_task.csv`, we will
look at the relationship between stem length and stem dry mass for the year 2004.

We will model the relationship with the based R `lm()` function.

$Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_i + e_i$

where $Y_i$ is the dependent or response variable, $\beta_0$ is the model intercept, 
$\beta_1$ is the model slope, $X_i$ is the independent or explanatory variable, 
and $e_i$ is the model error term.

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# install.packages("broom") To install broom package if not installed.

## bring the libraries into R
library(tidyverse)
library(cowplot)
library(broom)

# Load data
plant_test_data <- read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/plant_calcium_task.csv") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(watershed = recode(watershed, "W2" = "W1"),
                watershed = as.factor(watershed),
                transect  = as.factor(transect)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(stem_dry_mass < 1 & year == 2004)


```

Here, the dependent or explanatory variable is `stem_length`, and the independent or
response variable is `stem_dry_mass`.

To go from the English language research question to being ready to approach this 
question statistically we need to do a few things, namely:

- Decide on a suitable model: Here we are going to start with the belief that a 
simple straight line model will be suitable.
- State the null and alternative hypotheses.
- Decide on the significance level.

Optional: If you would like to have a go at any of these you are welcome to do so, 
otherwise you can unhide our version detailed below.

<details>
<summary><strong>Show answer</strong></summary>

- Regression equation (in context): $Mass = \beta_0 + \beta_1 Length + \epsilon$, 

$\epsilon \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$

- Null hypothesis ($H_0$): $\beta_1 = 0$, there is no association between 
between stem length and stem dry mass in 2004.

- Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$): $\beta_1 \ne 0$, there is an association between 
between stem length and stem dry mass in 2004.

- We will evaluate these with a significance level ($\alpha$) of 0.05 as this is 
standard sciences research question.

</details>


### Visualisation {.unnumbered}

The figure below provides an overview of three key descriptions we should include 
when presenting any scatterplot. Additionally, if extremes or potential outliers 
are present these should also be described and checked for validity (data entry 
mistake, measurement errors, units not a part of the population of interest, etc).

Let's visualise the data with the aim to check if a linear relationship is 
suitable and to describe the data (shape, direction, strength and potential extremes).

```{r}

plant_test_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass)) +
  geom_point() + # points for a scatterplot
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of stem length and stem dry mass in 2004",
       x = "Stem length (cm)",
       y = "Stem dry mass (g)") +
  theme_bw() 

```
Optional: We recommend you have a go at describing the scatterplot, then you can 
unhide our version detailed below.

**What is the relationship you see when plotting stem length with stem dry mass?**

<details>
<summary><strong>Show answer</strong></summary>

This relationship appears linear, positive and moderate with no potential extreme 
values.

</details>


### Assumptions {.unnumbered}

Let's create the additional visualisations to allow us to evaluate the assumptions.

The figures below are as follows:

- The fitted values versus the standardised residuals. This plot visualises 
**change in the standardised residuals over the range of the fitted values** 
to support an assessment of the assumption of equal variances. There should be an 
equal number of residual above zero and below zero, and not too many standardised 
residuals more extreme than -2 and 2. 

- A quantile–quantile (QQ) plot is a visualisation to check whether a 
**set of values (e.g. residuals from fitting a linear regression model) follows a particular distribution** 
(e.g. the normal distribution). The QQ plot which compares the theoretical quantiles 
from the normal distribution (x-axis) and sample standardised residuals presented 
as quantiles (y-axis) and is used to assess if the residuals are normally distributed. 
If the points follow the line then this is consistent with the residuals coming 
from a normal distribution. Systematic curvature (an S-shape) suggests the residuals 
may be skewed or have heavier or lighter tails than a normal distribution while a 
few points far from the line at the ends may indicate outliers or unusually large 
residuals.

- Optional: The plot of leverage versus the standardised residuals allows us to 
check if there are any large leverage points (leverage is how far a data point’s 
predictor values are from the “center” of all predictors) which also have large 
residuals. If there are any points with a large leverage and large residuals, 
these points are having an impact on the model and should be investigated further.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 3


## Run an initial the model
stem_lm <- lm(stem_dry_mass ~ stem_length , data = plant_test_data)

## Secondly create a set of visualisations that help us understand the diagnostics
### Get several key outputs including:
### - fitted values (.fitted)
### - standardised residuals (.std.resid)
### - leverage (.hat)
stem_aug <- broom::augment(stem_lm) 

diag_1 <- ggplot(stem_aug, aes(x = .fitted, y = .std.resid)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() +
  geom_hline(yintercept  = 0)+
  geom_hline(yintercept  = c(-2, 2), linetype  =3) +
  labs(title = "Fitted values vs std. residuals",
       x = "Fitted values",
       y = "Standardised residuals")

diag_2 <- ggplot(stem_aug, aes(sample = .std.resid)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "QQ plot of the residuals",
        x = "Theoretical Quantiles",
       y = "Standardised residuals")

diag_3 <- ggplot(stem_aug, aes(x = .hat, y = .std.resid)) + 
  geom_point() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Leverage vs std. residuals",
        x =  "Leverage",
       y = "Standardised residuals")

cowplot::plot_grid(diag_1, diag_2, diag_3, ncol = 3)

```


| Assumption                     | Check                                     | Met                |                              
|:------------------------------:|:-----------------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Linearity                      | In the scatterplot of stem length and stem dry mass we see a linear relationship  | This assumption is met.|
| Equal variances                | In the plot of fitted values vs the standardised residuals we see a similar spread of residual for all fitted values.  | This assumption is met. 
| Normally distributed residuals | In the QQ plot we see that there is good agreement between the theoretical and observed standardised residuals. |This assumption is met. |
| Influential points             | In the plot of leverage versus the standardised residuals the points with the largest leverage (influence) have small residuals |We do not have any concerning (high leverage) observations. |
| Independence                   | This data is from 2004 which is time series data, there may be some concerns about independence (if you included the other years) | This assumption needs a caveat. |

This analysis can proceed with a caveat on independence.

### Modelling {.unnumbered}

We can now get R to summarise and visualise the model so we can review.

```{r}
## summarise the model
summary(stem_lm)
confint(stem_lm)

## visualise the model
plant_test_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = stem_length, y = stem_dry_mass)) +
  geom_point() + # points for a scatterplot
  geom_smooth(method = lm, se = F, colour = "#e82c4a") +
  labs(title = "Scatterplot of stem length and stem dry mass in 2004",
       x = "Stem length (cm)",
       y = "Stem dry mass (g)") +
  theme_bw()

```

In looking at the output from R we see that a simple linear regression model 
was fitted to examine the relationship between stem length and stem dry mass. 
We will focus on understanding the coefficients and the R-squared. The fitted 
model can be written as:

$\widehat{Mass} = -0.04 + 0.001 \times Length$

The intercept (-0.04) represents the estimated stem dry mass when the stem length 
is 0 cm. The slope coefficient for stem dry mass is 0.0013, indicating that for each 
centimeter increase in stem length, the expected stem dry mass increase by 
approximately 0.001 grams, on average. If the model assumptions hold, we are 95% 
confident the true intercept lies between 0.0011 and 0.0015.

The coefficient for temperature is statistically significant (the probability value 
or *p*-value is small, $p < 0.001$), providing strong evidence that stem length 
is associated with stem dry mass in this dataset. The model has an $R^2$ value of 0.6, 
meaning that approximately 60% of the variability in stem dry mass is explained by 
stem length.

In preparation for more advanced modelling, we note that the overall F-test for 
the model is significant ($F(1,116) = 172.5$, $p < 0.001$), indicating that the 
regression model provides a better fit to the data than a model with no predictors.


### Interpretation {.unnumbered}

![](images/base_communicate.png)

**Publication-ready methods description**

To examine the relationship between sugar maples (*Acer saccharum*) stem length (cm) 
and stem dry mass (g) for the sampling year 2004, we (or I) constructed a linear
model using the base R 'lm()' function. Stem length was the independent variable, and 
stem dry mass was the dependent variable. A linear model was appropriate for the analysis
because model assumptions of linearly, equal variance, and leverage were met. Year 
of sampling may be a potential confound of true independence sampling which should
be of careful interpretation. The significance threshold (α) was set at 0.05. 
Analyses were conducted in R (version X.X.X).

**Publication-ready methods description**

A full interpretation of a regression model includes:

- A conclusion with respect to the null hypothesis, supported by a p-value
- A summary of what we learn from the modelling (slope and associated confidence interval)
- Any assumptions or caveats made along the way
- Optional: Interpretation of r-squared

You can write the results section like this:

We have evidence against the null hypothesis that there is no relationship between
stem length and stem dry mass (*F*~(1,116)~ = 172.5, *p* <0.001). 
For a one centimeter increase in stem length we see a 0.0013 g increase in stem 
dry mass ($\beta_0$ = -0.04, $\beta_1$ = 0.0013 [95% CI 0.0011–0.0015]; Fig. xxx). 60% of 
the variation in stem dry mass can be explained by stem length This assumes the 
sampling year or 2004 are representative of all years sampled.

## Two independent samples t-test

The two independent samples t-test is a statistical technique used to **compare two groups**, 
specifically we test of the mean of the two groups could be the same or if the two 
groups require separate means (the two groups are different statistically). 
In ecological research, this would be useful for comparing two groups such as a 
native and restored vegetation.

In this section we will investigate the impact of invasive species on the number 
of native species observed, by quadrant, comparing an area with this invasive species 
and an area without it.

We will model the relationship with the based R `t.test()` function.

**Research question*: Has there been an impact of the invasive species on the 
number of native plant species at the quadrant level?

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

## bring the libraries into R
library(tidyverse)

## bring the data into R from GitHub
invaded <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/invaded.csv", stringsAsFactors = T)

```

As this data is simulated for the purposes of learning we will focus on the process 
running a t-test in R and how to write an interpretation.


🧪 **Excerise: Write the null and alternative hypothesis for this data. Select a significance level**

<details>
<summary><strong>Show answer</strong></summary>

Null hypothesis ($H_0$): $\mu_{invasive} = \mu_{native}$, the population means 
of the number of native plant species in the quadrants in the areas with the 
invasive species and without the invasive species are the same.

Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$): $\mu_{invasive} < \mu_{native}$, the population 
means of the number of native plant species in the quadrants in the areas with the 
invasive species is less than the number in the areas without the invasive species. 

We will evaluate this with a significance level($\alpha$) of 0.05.

</details>

### Visualisation {.unnumbered}

![](images/base_visual.png)

Look at the data, then visualise the data to understand it, check for **extremes** 
and check the **assumptions** of a two independent samples t-test. We will also 
calculate some descriptive statistics. 

```{r}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4

## look at the data structure
glimpse(invaded)

## try both histograms and a comparative box and whisker plot to see which is nicer
hist_plot <- ggplot(data = invaded, aes(x = Native_count)) +
  geom_histogram(breaks  = seq(7,22,2)) + 
  facet_wrap(~ Group, ncol = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Comparative histograms",
       x = "Number of native species",
       y = "Frequency")

box_plot <- ggplot(data = invaded, aes(x= Group, y = Native_count)) +
  geom_boxplot() + 
  theme_bw() +
  labs(title = "Comparative box and whisker plot",
       x = '',
       y = "Number of native species",)

cowplot::plot_grid(hist_plot, box_plot, ncol = 2)
```


### Assumptions {.unnumbered}

| Assumption | Check         | Met       |                              
|:----------:|:-----------------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Equal variances    | In the plots the spread looks similar in the two groups (invaded and uninvaded) and the standard deviations are similar (2.89 and 2.84 for invaded and uninvaded respectively)  | This assumption is met.      |
| Normally distributed residuals   | Histogram suggests the data is symmetric to some extent and fairly bell-shaped measurements for both groups, and the sample size is the same in each group. |This assumption is met. |
| Independence      | This data simulated, we can assume independence. | This assumption is not relevant.

### Modelling {.unnumbered}

```{r}

## Run the t test, account for the one-side alternative hypothesis
t.test(Native_count ~ Group , data = invaded, alternative = c("less"))

```

### Interpretation {.unnumbered}

![](images/base_communicate.png)

**Publication-ready methods description**

To determine whether biological invasion was associated with reduced native species 
richness, native species counts were compared between invaded and uninvaded sites 
using a Welch's two-sample t-test. Welch's test was used because it is robust to 
unequal variances and sample sizes between groups. The model was constructed with 
the base R 't.test()' function. A directional (one-tailed) test was performed 
based on the a priori prediction that invaded sites would contain 
fewer native species than uninvaded sites. The significance threshold (α) was set at 0.05. 
Analyses were conducted in R (version X.X.X).

**Publication-ready results description**

Native species counts were significantly lower in invaded sites (mean ± s.d. = 13.1 ± 2.9) 
than in uninvaded sites by an average of 2 species (15.8 ± 2.6; Welch's two-sample 
*t*-test: *t* = -3.20, *df* = 41.69, *p* = 0.0013; Fig. xxx).

To find the descriptive statistics by the two groups, you can run the code here:

```{r}

invaded %>%
  group_by(Group) %>%
  summarise(mean = mean(Native_count),
            sd = sd(Native_count),
            n = n())

```



## One-way ANOVA

A one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) is a statistical technique used to 
**compare the means of three or more groups**. Specifically, it tests whether a
ll groups could share the same population mean or whether at least one group has a 
different mean from the others. In ecological research, this would be useful for 
comparing several groups, such as plant growth in native, restored, and degraded 
vegetation sites.

We will model the relationship with the based R `aov()` function, but you can also 
use the `lm()` function as well. ANOVA is a linear regression BUT the predictor 
variables are categorical rather than continuous. Moreover, instead of a slope, 
with ANOVA you obtain an estimate of the response variable for each explanatory 
variable category.

In this example we will focus on the effects altitude on species richness using 
simulated data with  three altitude bands: low, mid, and high elevation.

**Research question**: Has there been an impact of altitude on the plant species richness?

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}

## bring the libraries into R
library(tidyverse)

## bring the data into R
altitude <- read.csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/altitude.csv", stringsAsFactors = F)

## make altitude a factor with the ordering low, mid and high 
## Note: R otherwise will use alphabetical ordering

altitude <- altitude %>%
  mutate(Altitude = factor(Altitude , levels = c("Low", "Mid", "High")))

```

As this data is simulated for the purposes of learning we will focus on the process 
running one-way ANOVA in R and learning how to write an interpretation.

🧪 **Exerise: Write the null and alternative hypothesis for this data. Select a significance level**

<details>
<summary><strong>Show answer</strong></summary>

Null hypothesis ($H_0$): $\mu_{low} = \mu_{mid} = \mu_{high}$, the population 
means of the number of  plant species in low, mid and high altitude regions are 
the same.

Alternative hypothesis ($H_1$): At least one altitude region is different.

We will evaluate this with a significance level($\alpha$) of 0.05.

</details>

### Visualisation {.unnumbered}

![](images/base_visual.png)

```{r}
## look at the data a couple of different ways
glimpse(altitude)

## the descriptive stats (you can use describe if you prefer)
altitude %>%
  group_by(Altitude)  %>%
  summarise(
    mean_richness = mean(Richness),
    sd_richness = sd(Richness),
    n = n())

## try  box and whisker plot and put the points in too
ggplot(altitude, aes(x = Altitude, y = Richness)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.1, alpha = 0.6) +
  labs(
    title = "Species richness across altitude",
    x = "Altitude",
    y = "Species Richness"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

```

### Assumptions {.unnumbered}

| Assumption | Check         | Met       |                              
|:----------:|:-----------------------------------------:|:------------------:|
| Equal variances    | In the plots the spread looks similar in the three groups (Low, Mid and High) and the standard deviations are similar (4.91, 4.18 and 4.35 for Low, Mid and High respectively). The ratio of the largest sd to the smallest sd is 4.91/3.18 = 1.17 which is less than 2.  | This assumption is met.      |
| Normally distributed residuals   | Box and whisker plots with the data suggests symmetric and fairly bell-shaped measurements for all groups, and the sample size is the same in each group. |This assumption is met. |
| Independence      | This data simulated, we can assume independence. | This assumption is not relevant.

### Modelling {.unnumbered}

::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

### Using aov()

The code runs the ANOVA test, analysing species richness (Richness) as a function 
of (~) altitude (Altitude), getting data (data = ...) from the data frame altitude.

The `summary()` function shows you the summary output of your ANOVA, also known 
as your ANOVA table, with degrees of freedom, F value and p value (all the info we need!).

```{r}

## Run the one-way ANOVA
altitude_aov <- aov(Richness ~ Altitude, data = altitude)
summary(altitude_aov)

## as the overall p-value is significant we can also run post hoc tests
TukeyHSD(altitude_aov)

```

### Using lm()

If you want more details about your analysis, you can run the same code but using 
a `lm()` linear model function. As mentioned above, ANOVA is in itself a linear model.

```{r}

## Run the one-way ANOVA
altitude_lm <- lm(Richness ~ Altitude, data = altitude)
summary(altitude_lm)

```
::: 

### Interpretation {.unnumbered}

::: {.panel-tabset .nav-pills}

### Using aov()

**Publication-ready methods description**

To investigate whether species richness varied with altitude, a one-way analysis 
of variance (ANOVA) was performed with altitude category (Low, Mid, and High) 
as a fixed dependent factor and species richness as the response variable. 
The model was constructed with the base R 'aov()' function.
The ANOVA tested for differences in mean richness among altitude categories. 
Prior to analysis, ANOVA assumptions of independence, normality of residuals,
and homogeneity of variances were assessed using diagnostic plots and formal tests 
where appropriate.

Following a significant overall effect, Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) 
tests were used to identify which altitude categories differed from one 
another while accounting for multiple comparisons. The significance threshold (α) 
was set at 0.05. Analyses were conducted in R (version X.X.X).


**Publication-ready results description**

Species richness differed significantly among altitude categories (one-way ANOVA: 
*F*~(2,87)~ = 92.65, *p* < 0.001). Altitude explained a substantial proportion 
of the variation in species richness.

Post hoc Tukey's HSD tests revealed significant differences among all altitude 
categories (p < 0.001 for all comparisons; Fig. xxx). Species richness was significantly 
higher at mid-altitude sites than at low-altitude sites (mean difference = 8.13 species, 
95% CI = 5.36–10.89). High-altitude sites had significantly lower richness than both 
low-altitude sites (mean difference = −7.64 species, 95% CI = −10.41 to −4.88) and 
mid-altitude sites (mean difference = −15.77 species, 95% CI = −18.53 to −13.01). 
Overall, species richness was greatest at mid-altitude sites and lowest at high-altitude 
sites.

### Using lm()

**Publication-ready methods description**

The relationship between altitude and species richness was assessed using a 
linear model with species richness as the response variable and altitude category 
(Low, Mid, and High) as the predictor. Altitude was treated as a categorical factor, 
with low altitude specified as the reference category. Model coefficients therefore 
represented the difference in mean species richness between the reference category 
and each of the other altitude categories. The model was constructed with the base 
R 'lm()' function.

Model significance was evaluated using an F-test, and the significance of individual 
altitude categories was assessed using t-tests on the estimated regression coefficients. 
Model fit was quantified using the coefficient of determination (R^2^). 
Prior to analysis, assumptions of linear regression, including independence of observations, 
normality of residuals, and homogeneity of variance, were assessed using diagnostic plots. 
The significance threshold (α) was set at 0.05. Analyses were conducted in R (version X.X.X).


**Publication-ready results description**

There was a significant effect of altitude on species richness (*F*~(2,87)~ = 92.65, 
*p* < 0.001; Fig. xxx), which explained 68.1% of the variation in richness (R^2^ = 0.68).
Using low-altitude sites as the reference category, species richness was 
significantly higher at mid-altitude sites, which supported on average 8.13 more 
species than low-altitude sites ($\beta_1$ = 8.13 ± 1.16 SE, *t* = 7.01, *p* < 0.001). 
In contrast, high-altitude sites supported significantly fewer species than 
low-altitude sites, with richness being 7.64 species lower on average 
($\beta_1$ = −7.64 ± 1.16 SE, *t* = −6.60, *p* < 0.001). 

:::

:::

# Writing Results {.unnumbered}

In a scientific report you must always present:

- The **direction** of the change (e.g. increase or decrease, higher or lower).
- the **magnitude** of the change (how big the different is, or how step is the slope).
- the **statistical support** (statistical outcomes and level of significance; 
t-value, R^2^, *p*-values).
- a visualisation of the outcome (e.g. scatterplot, boxplot, dot plots etc).
- any assumptions or caveats made along the way.

Full description is provided in the report guideline. For example:
*"Seedlings from the drought treatment grew twice as slow compared to the control* 
*water-treated seedlings (control = 3 ± 0.45 mm/day, drought = 1.5 ± 0.31 mm/day;* 
*t~53~ = 5.06, p = <0.0001; Fig 2)"*

# Why Log scale {.unnumbered}

In many ecological systems, such as island size, values often are **non-linear** 
which does not meet the assumptions of linear models (like in this prac). 
Many small islands vs few large islands.


If you tried to fit island size with species richness, it wont work well because 
the relationship is curved (**left figure**). If you log transform island size 
(island_area_log) and species richness (species_richness_log), the relationship 
looks more linear (**right figure**).

```{r log fig, echo=FALSE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3


library(cowplot)

island <- read.csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nicholaswunz/ECS200-Workshop/refs/heads/main/data/island.csv')

raw_plot <- island %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = exp(island_area_log), y = species_richness)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ log(x),
              se = FALSE, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Raw un-transformed data",
       x = "Island size (km)",
       y = "Species richness") +
  theme_classic()


log_plot <- island %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = island_area_log, y = species_richness_log)) +
  geom_point() +
  stat_smooth(method = "lm", se = F, colour = "black") +
  labs(title = "Transformed data",
       x = "Island size (log)",
       y = "Species richness (log)") +
  theme_classic()

cowplot::plot_grid(raw_plot, log_plot, ncol = 2)

```


By log transforming:

- It **stabilises variance**: Ecological data often have variance that increases 
with the mean (e.g., larger islands have both more species and more variability). 
Raw data has fan-shaped” spread while log transforming evens the spread
- it reduces the influence of **extreme values**.
- It **improves interpretability** of parameters: The slope z becomes a scaling 
exponent.
- It often makes data more **“normal”**: Many statistical methods assume normally 
distributed residuals. Log transformation can reduce skewness

When *not* to log-transform:

- You have zeros like count data (can't log zeros).
- The relationship is already linear.
- Interpretation on the original scale is critical.


If you need to log transform your data, here is how to do it:

```{r log, eval=FALSE}

# new_data is whatever data object you have
# x_value is whatever the name of the data column you want to log transform.

new_data <- new_data %>%
  mutate(x_value_log = log(x_value))

```

